# I Reviewed 100k-Star Skills...

**Channel:** dreadjordan
**Source:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eg0Q1TrCaEs

---

Pretty much every top repo you can find—Karpathy skills and you have Anthropic's on posted skills—seems to be a very hot topic. The question is: are skills good, or are skills the new snake oil? In this video, I want to take a look at a few skill repos. I want to read through these skills line for line and go in with a pretty objective mindset of: would this be actually valuable for the LM, or are people just selling us handwritten essays falsely claiming to be an improvement?

Before we dive in, I think it's good for us to get kind of a baseline idea of skills. If you're not familiar with skills, it is an MD file, such as this one, which is fed into your agent. This is Matt PCO's "ask Matt" skill. When you're targeting this skill, the LM is going to literally call the skill every single time. You can kind of view it as just a standard prompt that you send at the beginning of your prompt window.

There's this article here from UC Irvine that discusses skills.md. It's titled "From Anatomy to Smells: An Empirical Study of skill.md in Agent Skills." It's a relatively new article from July of this year, and they're really harping on this term "skill smell." To me, that is what we're going to be investigating—seeing if we can uncover any of that in the skills that we're about to introduce. As we discussed, the skills file really provides a prompt that gets repeated on each request, allowing you to effectively fine-tune the way it does things.

Now, there are some absolute nuances to that, which is why we're investigating this. It goes on to mention that the way you write these skills can have an impact on their effectiveness. Every line that you're adding to the skill has a chance of negatively impacting the output. There are different types of skills. For instance, "ask Matt" would be—I imagine this skill is not meant to be used for active development; it's more of a router of skill for skills. But let's see if we can find one that's more intended to be used during development. This might be diagnosing bugs. This skill here even describes it: "a diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regression." You use `/debug` this or whatever, and it'll execute this skill.

I don't want to read through this yet because I want us to get a good understanding of the pitfalls of skills before we actually go in and read. This paper talks about how to identify skill smell. This is what we're primarily going to start with. The part that interests us the most here is going to be in the methodology. They describe how skill smell falls into two categories: statically detectable smells and semantically detectable smells.

An oversized skill would fall under the statically detectable realm. They call it specifically here: 5,000 words. That would be considered a smell just based off the sheer size. Then the second category is semantically detectable, which requires a bit more of contextual reasoning. They don't go into full depth of how they measure this, but they do call out that the semantically detectable is just based on the context of the file. What I assume they're doing, based on the way they describe it here, is looking for contradictions and anti-patterns—things that would be deemed as bad engineering behavior.

I imagine would also fall under that "prompt debt," which is a comprehensive study of technical debt across LM projects. It really just describes the hierarchy of impactful factors when it comes to technical debt with LM. The main area that we want to focus on here is on the developer. Some technical debt is introduced by the model provider, but in the case of instructions and skill.md, these are very much on the developer itself and can introduce a lot of technical debt there.

Here we can see a table that goes into the percentage of impact for technical debt. At the very top here we have prompt debt, which really is part of the skill and instruction file. Effectively, this could be bundled into this high count here. It cites prompt debt as being prompt debt here, and it talks about optimizing prompt design. Their data set revealed that LM developers often struggle to craft prompts that achieve desired outcomes, following a correct format, and managing the prompt length, which can directly influence the LM's performance for a given task.

This is primarily the concern we're going to have here with these skills.md: are they shooting us in the foot when it comes to performance and the overall end result? There's also the factor of cost. Are these skills increasing our costs? Are they making it more expensive to run our task? Later in the paper, it discusses instruction blocks. In particular here: "unclear suboptimal instructions coupled with overly long prompt instructions can severely impact the effectiveness of LM responses by leading to misinterpretation or incomplete task execution."

With that in mind, I think the skill smells that we're looking for are length and contradictions. That is pretty much what we gathered from the papers we just read. But I really think there's another one here that I haven't seen talked about, and so I'm going to add this as my own skill smell. I'm going to coin this one "human fluff."

What I mean by this: first of all, LMs are not human. Yes, they're trained on our text, but there's certain text and descriptions that it is never going to understand at the level that a human does. There's certain keywords that it knows in this model—frameworks, API, `useEffect`, `useState`, and so on. These are the things it knows. Well, yes, it can take something that it's not familiar with and translate it. If you were to say something like "send a request for the name," you don't necessarily have to specify specifically that you're calling an API; it'll pick up on this. But it does have to do some kind of translation from a human language into something that would actually be relevant given the context.

When I say human fluff, I'm really saying words that just add confusion to the end-to-end. This is something that I'm going to look out for, and I think will be a big part here increasing our technical debt just because we're treating it like it's a human being.

Let's get into this here. We're going to start with Andre Karpathy skills. Now, from my understanding, this is not his repo. Somebody just made this repo based on his philosophies with agents. It even says here in the about section: "a single cloud.md file to improve upon cloud code behavior derived from Andre Karpathy's observations." So this is not from Karpathy himself, but it's based on observations of LM coding pitfalls. These are very popular repos—195,000 stars, freaking millions of forks. A lot of these authors like to make sure their Twitters are at the top.

We'll go to the cloud.md. This has the skills itself. Right off the bat: 2.3 kilobytes. A skill smell was defined as a file exceeding 5,000 words. If we treat 5,000 tokens as the guiding star—here's an image, by the way, that can give you an idea of what we're looking at—5,000 tokens is about an essay's worth, a little bit over an essay's worth. Ideally, when we're looking at these, we want to evaluate how much before and after that is.

We're going to get a token analyzer. There's this tokenizer here from OpenAI; we're going to use this. Okay, and so this one falls at about 520. In terms of length, this is a good length. I think we can give this a check mark in terms of its ability to have a length. Just so we can keep track of this, let's do "Karpathy skill smell," and I think we can give the length a check mark.

Let's read this line by line. I encourage you to think about this as we go through. We've already verified that the length is good, but let's think about contradictions. Let's think about human fluff. Are we saying things that may not translate well to a trained database on code?

It starts off: "Behavioral guidelines to reduce common LM coding mistakes merge with project specific instructions as needed. Trade-off these guideline bias toward caution over speed for trivial tasks. Use judgment." Right off the bat, I think this part probably wouldn't be a good idea to include. Part of why I say that is I would deem this to be human fluff. "Behavioral guidelines to reduce common LM coding mistakes"—this is putting a lot of weight on the LM. As a human being, do you understand what this means right away? I would say this is very broad and not clear. I'm just envisioning this: we need to realize these LMs operate best with clear instruction, and this is not clear at all. I would instantly lose some points there, but let's continue. If it were me personally, I think I would just omit this section.

Number one: "Think before coding. Before implementing, state your assumptions explicitly. If uncertain, ask. If multiple interpretations exist, present them. Don't pick silent. If a simpler approach exists, say so. Push back when warranted. If something is unclear, stop. Ask." When I'm reading this, I'm immediately assuming the LM is just going to ask a [ __ ] ton of questions. How is it going to be able to determine certainty here? "State your assumptions explicitly, and if you're uncertain, ask." If it's uncertain, I don't think it would even execute on the operation to begin with. When it reads this, I have a feeling it's just going to constantly assume it's uncertain. We've also said "ask" twice. This to me is just going to have the LM asking pretty much everything at every step without any rhyme or reason. The LM's really just going to look at this, and then the rest is just—who cares? These are all [snorts] do not care. Just fluff to the LM. Whatever. Who cares? This is what matters: we're just going to ask him about this every time.

We can also see really there's some inconsistency here because we're telling the LM, "hey, think before you code," which is really a careful approach. Then we're later down the line "goal-driven execution," which is really goal-driven. These two can't coexist well because you're saying we're going based off exit criteria—that is our guiding star—but then earlier you just got done saying that our guiding star was asking the user. You can absolutely envision a case where it's just picking: "hey, do I just listen to this step here or do I go to this one?"

Another concern I have, which I would consider human fluff, is the idea of "simplicity first." This adds a little bit of concern on maintainability. I can envision a lot of cases where, depending on the model you're using, this may take it to mean, "hey, we don't need to worry about maintainability here; we can stuff all this into one file and care little about the readability just because we want simple." Even outside of this, I would consider this human fluff, but then we go deeper and we see terminology like this: "Touch only what you must clean up your own mess." What does this mean? This is what I mean by human fluff. When we tell a human being about "mess," it's usually pretty obvious what we're talking about, but how is an LLM going to be able to determine what mess looks like? You're running the risk of the LM interpreting mess as something that's actually intended for maintainability. And also, you're kind of assuming the LM is making a mess to begin with. I would assume

This wouldn't be the case. And just taking a step back here, I have concerns about this really just slowing us down, right? I encourage you to try this skill, but what you're going to find is that it asks for every [ __ ] thing. This portion here makes the biggest impact and it makes me wonder like what's the point in the LM? Like I get it. There are points to this and I get what it's trying to do, right? It wants you to feel more connected to the codebase.

And so for Carpathy skills, I would give this a 6 out of 10. I feel as though it's using a little bit of too—it's using too much human fluff. I really think having it ask questions is just going to result in really ruining the development experience and adding no real value. I think I saw some contradictions in there. 6 out of 10 seems like a fair score.

And so the next set of skills we're going to look at are the Matt PCO skills. His are very famous on the internet. In fact, I think his entire business model now is selling people on skills. I don't know if he sells the skills or if he just sells his courses still. But definitely this is like 99% of what he talks about.

And before we get into that, um there's this article here from Alan Chan. Something I really really want to read before we get to it because to me it's—it's a common occurrence is this illusion of control. You know, at the end of the day, an LM is undeterministic, right? There are certain things you can do to make it as close to as possible is deterministic, but at the end of the day, it's still undeterministic, right? We know that for a fact.

And so, a common trend that I see, and I think hopefully you'll see as well when we observe the Carpathy or sorry, the PCO skills, it has a tendency to feel as though it's gaining some control. PCO's repo um even calls it out: "skills for real engineers. Use it for real engineering, not vibe coding." Right? Really he sells you on this idea that you have more control by utilizing his skills. And I really just wanted to read this before we dive in cuz I think it's important to call out.

And so he says, "Let me show you a real example. Below is a simplified version of an actual production agent prompt I encountered reduced from 200 lines to the highlight the core pattern." And you can see there's this, you know, absolute slopfest of instruction files here. And he goes into how he identifies kind of this concept of skill slop. So he calls out an anti pattern of a brittle prompt, right? Treating a prompt as a stable contract when minor wording changes silently break behavior.

This is a huge part of why skills are risky, right? It's this assumption that it's a contract that the LM is just going to abide by at all stops. Unfortunate is even the model you use, right? You could send the same skills.md to a different model and it's going to behave entirely different. And he goes on to say, right, the prompt appears to work and it might work a good bit, but you're not going to notice when it tits up and it's actually negatively impacting your your end result. And with it being, you know, a very non-deterministic thing, you will not find this out right away.

And so this is the anti-pattern that I really wanted to call out was this probabilistic rule engine. And I think we may see this with Matt PCO skills. I will I will say our uh newer models are a lot better at listening to skills and instructions, but at the end of the day, when [ __ ] hits the fan and you have a lot going on, the agent isn't going to be able to do this at a high rate.

All right, so we'll start off. We'll go into his engineering skills, right? "Skills for real engineers," as he calls them. And so we'll go into the implement skill cuz I think this will be the most interesting. And so this is I'm assuming the skill that is for implementing the code. Okay, so this appears to be a router to Jesus, man. See, we've got like these freaking complex architectures for [ __ ] skills at this point. So, it says implement a piece of work based on a spec or a set of tickets. Use / TDD or possible. Sure, what this is referring to. Okay, TDD. Oh, test-driven development, of course. Okay.

Okay. So, this is the one we're going to focus on. Um, looking at the size of it, it looks pretty good. Let's do a test here. Uh, so it is a bit larger than the Carpathy skills, but it is still quite small. And so, we'll read through it. So description: test-driven development used when the user wants to build features or fix bugs. Test first mentions red green refactor or wants integration test. Okay. TDD is the red to green loop. This skill is a reference that makes that loop produce tests worth keeping. What a good test is where tests go. The any patterns and the rules of the loop. Every section applies on every cycle. Consult them before and during the loop not after.

Okay. So my first question is what is a good test? I'm assuming. Yep. Okay. So he instantly goes into that right after. When exploring the codebase, read context.md. So test names and interface vocabulary match the project's domain language and respect ADRs in the area you're touching. My only complaint here is that description kind of already covers this, right? I think LLMs are well aware of what test-driven development is. Feel like you could go straight into what a good test is, but maybe there's something I'm missing on that nuance.

It goes on to say tests verify behavior through public interfaces, not implementation details. Code can change entirely. Tests shouldn't. A good test reads like a specification. "User can check out with valid cart." Tells you exactly what capability exists and survives refactors because it doesn't care about the internal structure and then it's pointing to some more MD files for guidelines. And so while this skill here is a pretty good size, I imagine it's going to add up a lot as we go down into these skills, right? Test.md. This is another oh 77 line. Is this referencing anything else? Okay. And then mocking.md.

So assuming it reads all three of these, you're looking at about about five or 6 kilobytes, maybe even a little bit more that are sent each time. But let's go ahead and try out the tokenizer. So this will be for the main skill. It's so so weird that we're having to go through nested skills, but okay, thousand. Okay, so [clears throat] we're looking at about 1522 each time. Okay, so size-wise, it's not too bad. You're definitely under a penny in terms of each each time it costs you to send this.

Um, again, I feel like LM's really already understand. It really feels like we're doing some unnecessary lecturing here, right? An LM already knows what test-driven development is. This part here when exploring the codebase read context.md if it exists. This could be okay, right? Because if we're working with an LM that's not naturally going to this, this is valid. But I would say this part here and this part here is literally just code smell at that point.

And kind of, you know, what we discussed earlier about this illusion of control. I think we really want to believe that we can control the LM in this way, right? "Every section applies to every cycle. Consult them before and during." Reality is, yeah, this might work on occasion, but the LM is not going to listen to you at every step of the way, right? This is just not going to happen. LM will sometimes listen to this. Now, that's not to say it's useless. Like I said, I think the LM will listen to this on occasion. It definitely steers.

But if you really think throwing this into your project is going to result in a clear contract that is never violated, you're smoking a pipe. Right? Although we talked about how the skill kind of gets fed into every prompt, it's not getting fed in during each step. Right? So if you send your prompts, like let's say these are all of your prompts. Although it's true that it's going to slot in the skill in between each of these. We can view this dash line as the skill. It's going to send that in each prompt.

But you have to realize that this is going to execute a lot of subtasks. Right? But if we look at prompt one, there's a lot of tasks that are being executed after this prompt that it may or may not actually be sending that skill into. And so it's possible you run into a case where, hey, yeah, it listened to your skill for this subtask and it output some, you know, thing about the cycle and it listened to the cycle thing. But all these other ones, it's just going to disregard it and you're not going to even have control over that. That's out of your control. You can put as much words, fancy words as you want into a skill file, but it's not going to guarantee that.

And so I won't go into test.md, right? If we if we read through every one of his skills, we'd be here all day. He's got a lot of these, but I kind of just want to keep going through this one. He goes on to discuss seams, where tests go. A seam is the public boundary you test at the interface where you observe behavior without reaching inside. Test lives at seams, never against internal. So it feels like we're just repeating ourselves a bit here.

And again, kind of part of the complaint that I had with the Carpathy skill of shooting ourselves in the foot. It really feels like we're doing that here. Like I get it, you know, everyone wants to feel like they have control over their development progress. It's nice to feel like we have control, but at the end of the day, what is the benefit to an LM? It's speed, right? We would not be using these LMS today if we couldn't get quicker output.

And the reality is is you're not going to read through all this damn code anyway. I envision 99% of the users of this of this skill, they're just chalking it in in their codebase and then going back to autopilot. Somebody actually had this mindset of, oh, I want full control over my development process. I want to feel like, you know, I'm there every step of the way. I really don't think they would be using a skill like this.

And if we're going to rate PCO skills, say he also gets a pass on the length. I think there's definitely a good amount of length, especially when you're adding in nested skills like this. I know he's treating these as separate files, but literally the LM's just going to take these each time any which—I get it at this point. This is like a object object level programming, so it's trying to keep it clean and and separated. I get that. So I I wouldn't fault it there.

Contradictions. I actually think his contradiction level is pretty low. At least from this one that I'm reading here, I don't see anything that stands out to me as being a contradiction. And so he does have that advantage. He fluff is definitely here. I would say I would say there's a lot of tutorial speak in this, right? I really don't think we need to describe what test-driven development is to the LM. I think we're repeating it here.

I think when we say things like this, it adds no value to the LM whatsoever. Right? "The skills, the reference that makes the loop produce tests worth keeping." Like what does any of this stuff matter to the LM, right? This is assuming that the LM is a human being and that we can communicate to it like a tutorial. And so I would say human fluff is definitely there. Overall, from my read, I would say his skills are better than the Carpathy skill. It's an 8 out of 10.

And so if you asked me, right, which skill would I use? I think there's one worth mentioning, which is no skill at all. Right? Here's the thing about no skill at all. It passes on all these metrics. Now, I know that's being egregious, but I do want to point out that the LM comes packaged a certain way, right? You have to realize every model that you get, it's trained on data and it's designed a certain way. And every skills.md instructions file that you're adding on to it, it's adjusting its its behavior, its natural tendencies. And so, you are pretty much guaranteed introducing technical debt. It really

It does not matter what you put in the skills MD. There is some form of technical debt being introduced. Whether that's worth it depends on your use case, right? I think PCO is famous for having a skill called grill me. God, it's freaking nested depths of—okay, it's apparently impossible to find, so I'm not going to spend an hour trying to find it. But he does have certain skills that are fine-tuned for like learning purposes.

It's okay in certain contexts to introduce this technical debt as long as it's not intended for development. In my opinion, if you're doing anything for development, you should not be using a skill. Really, skills should be viewed as a mistake. If you feel the need to use a skill, that tells me either you're doing something weird that the LM doesn't know about or the LM is weird, which maybe that's fine and you're okay with that and you're willing to accept this technical debt that you're introducing.

But I still say skills should be treated as a mistake at the end of the day, right? If I could rename skills, I would just name it duct tape. But unfortunately, that doesn't work as well. Nobody wants to say they're adding duct tape to their LM. And this is basically what you're doing, right? You're doctoring your LM with these new instructions. It's really not going to listen to 100% of the time, but when it does, you're just snipping it, right? You're going against its natural tendencies.

And this paper here from uh Aman Meta—Meta, hope I'm pronouncing that okay—now, this kind of discusses the realities of using different LMS as well, right? Just because that skill works for say GPT does not mean it's going to work for an notice, right? Skill smells once they're there, they're there as we've discussed, right? It's going to keep sending that skill. And so every bit of smell that you have here is going to compound and compound and compound.

And really, I believe even in a perfect world, it doesn't make sense to use these as true beneficiaries. The amount of control here is very inconsistent. And so what you end up with is the LM sometimes listening and then sometimes not listening. So you end up with more inconsistency. Right? If I tell the LM, "hey, test-driven development, you know, here's what a good test is," it might listen a couple times, but then the other 10 times it didn't listen. And so now we have an inconsistent code base, right? We have a code base that's listening sometimes to these instructions but then going off and doing whatever it wants for the other.

And so overall I think skills should be viewed as technical debt. I think there's a place for them. I think there are cases where you might want one, right, for a very specific scenario or in the case of, you know, Matt HCO skills for learning purposes. I think when we view them for what they really are, which is just a bunch of human speak that claims that tries to steer the LLM to do something, but in reality, there's no—there's no contract here. This is not a contract. It's still probabilistic.

I also encourage you to realize a lot of the skill providers I find, they don't really code that much. I'm not going to go into that. Yeah. Anyway, I encourage you to think for yourself on this. I think the narrative that we're seeing going around of skills being this all great thing and a lot of people are profiting off of it and it's a dangerous realm to be in. But if we view it as, you know, technical debt, duct tape, I think we'll be in a good spot. Use it only when you need it. Don't use it ideally. Stick to what the LM knows and is good at. And only use skills MD where you're doing something weird or very context specific.

# "The engineer of the future is the person who is able to choose what is worth doing." — Addy Osmani

**Channel:** AI Engineer
**Source:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n97BCfyFIvw

---

**Speaker:** Howdy, folks. So, good afternoon or good whatever time it is when you're watching this on YouTube. I'm really excited to be here. And today I want to talk to you about really what it takes to keep the human in the loop where engineering is concerned. I really want to start with a human side before we talk about the architecture here.

I think that the engineer of the future is going to be really defined by the person who is able to choose what is worth doing. They're going to own the evidence. They're going to own the understanding as well as the verdict around increasingly automated work that's being done by agents. Now, when I use the term verdict, I don't mean that we're suddenly all going to be Judge Judy. We're not. But what I mean really is something just a little bit different. I mean, we're going to be accountable for the production decisions. Does something ship? Do we block it? Do we redirect it or accept the risk? Quality is something that we all talk about a lot, but quality produces evidence. A verdict assigns responsibility. And answerability is really what lets us stand behind a verdict.

And this of course is not the only way that our industry is starting to think about our roles evolving. Boris Cherney recently put some useful language around what many teams are starting to feel. The old craft boundaries are getting blurry, and roles are re-bumbling around the work itself. And the important question here becomes a lot less about what is your title and more what part of the system can you own? Now, I like this taxonomy quite a lot. It's optimistic without being overly vague. So, things like prototype, build, sweep, grow, and maintain. And these are real engineering modes. Agents are going to help with all of them, but the scarce thing is not merely doing the task. It's going to be knowing which mode your product needs and what quality bar applies and who owns the result at the end of the day.

Now, we've been talking about harnesses and loop engineering and software factories over the last couple of days. We can talk why this shift is happening. We moved past the model as the whole story, right? With harness engineering, the coding agent is the model plus the harness around it, right? Your context, your tools, your file system, Git. And the harness is what turns intelligence into something that you can delegate to.

The next move was loop engineering, where we weren't just prompting one run anymore. We were designing systems that kept prompting, checking, and remembering, and deciding what happened next. And that's really when agents started to feel like infrastructure. And once you start putting all of those things together, you get that software factory. Dex covered this well in his talk, where you have agents that are running inside that inner loop and evidence that comes out. Humans still end up making the production decisions in this loop. And the wind really isn't moving us from it. The wind is moving human judgments the highest leverage checkpoint, I think.

And this is why it starts to matter now. AI-generated and AI-assisted code is becoming normal code for a lot of us. One of Sonar's 2026 survey said that AI-assisted code is no longer marginal. It's increasingly having a large role in our code bases. And once that happens, answerability stops being this philosophical world. It becomes an engineering requirement.

And there's a quality point here as well, right? Like we used to care about clean code, code that people could read. But cleaner code is actually not just going to help the next human and the next person on your teams. It actually helps the next agent. Another one of Sonar's research studies found that clean and messy repos had roughly the same pass rates, but clean code actually used fewer tokens and caused fewer revisits. So there's a lot of benefit to maintainability that can fuel efficiency for your factories.

Now, making generation cheaper does not automatically make review cheaper, right? I think a lot of us are facing this moment and we know that engineers are not naive. The Sonar numbers say that almost everybody is skeptical of AI code. Now, I love working in my software factory. I love building my engineering loops. But the problem is still capacity. If 96% of people don't fully trust that code, but only about half always verify before committing, we have this danger that we've got distrust without bandwidth. And so safety comes from making verification cheaper, clearer, and harder for people to skip.

And if you zoom out from the individual reviewer to the organization, review and validation start becoming a bottleneck when governance isn't able to catch up and adoption is already moving way faster than any company can go and set their policies. And this means that we have some hard questions we have to deal with, like did a model actually touch this file? And the hard questions are also like what constraints guided that work? What evidence was produced? What risk was accepted and who owned the result?

Now, the agent can ship more than any of us can review, right? So what are we still good for? I think it's a question that's on a lot of our minds, right? And you know, if Homer Simpson's experience automating computers can teach us anything, maybe this is our future. I don't think it is. But it's one direction things could take. Now, let's try that again. If change is where humans enter the loop, if generation scales faster than comprehension, the scarce resource becomes judgment that's backed by evidence. So, the question is no longer how much can the agent do, but where does human judgment still create leverage?

Now, I want to talk to you about two terms that I'm going to use for the career part of this talk, alpha and decay. Alpha is the gap between what you can do today and what current models can do. That gap is a very real thing, and decay is the clock on that gap. If the thing that makes you special is a capability, the frontier is eventually going to come for it. Right? And there's a whole conversation around this.

This is one of the reasons why taste keeps coming up. Paul Graham had a point here that I think is very right. When anyone can make anything, choosing what to make becomes very important, and I buy that. But I also think that we have to be very careful because taste can become a magic word for whatever part of the work we don't want to explain just yet. Mitchell Hashimoto gave us a more useful version of this definition. Taste is the ability to make high-quality qualitative judgments where no objective metric exists yet. That matters because it puts taste before the benchmark and before the market has fully voted.

When you try out a model and you see the kind of UX and the kind of experiences that it builds, you can often tell when you think it has taste or lacks taste or where there's a gap there that humans can fill. Now, this is also only useful if we can turn some of this concept around taste into critique, examples, and better judgment over time. So, yes, taste matters when production gets cheaper. And if anyone can generate 10 options, the scarce skill is really knowing which option deserves to exist. But taste is not some eternal moat. It's alpha as well.

Now, the people with taste are still going to matter. I personally think they're still going to matter for a long time. But the best version of that skill is not mystique. It's making better calls and leaving behind examples that your team and the system can learn from. Now, let's apply the decay test. Well, we used to have speed. That decayed. We used to have recall. You know, harnesses have memory. Verification is moving into harnesses, evals, static checks, and model critique. Taste, I continue to think this is going to decay much more slowly, but it still resets as models learn from examples and preferences. Even judgment in some ways is a slope rather than a wall.

So, the strategy is not to cling to any one capability. It's for us to keep moving our edges up a level. So, this is one of the reasons why what can the agent do is not the best strategic question anymore. The list of things that agents can't do just keeps shrinking. The better question for us is really what can only a human be answerable for. Not because, you know, any of us are magical in any way, but because some decisions actually require ownership. They require context, risk acceptance, and responsibility after that work ships.

This is why the word engineer has to get just a little bit stricter. More people than ever can now make computers do things, and I think that's truly awesome. The total addressable market for builders has never been larger, and that's so cool. But it's a huge expansion of leverage. An engineer is not merely somebody who can code, you know, and get things to exist. An engineer can reason about systems. They think about constraints, you defend trade-offs, you can manage risk, and you're the person that can be reached out to when things start to break.

So, what are things that engineers should avoid if we want to stay effective and accountable in this moment? Well, the first thing to avoid really is cognitive debt. Now, cognitive debt is the erosion of your understanding and memory around how to solve problems. I think a lot of us start to feel this the more that we're using agents every single day. I know that I feel this a lot. And it's because we're deferring more and more to AI to solve our problems. For code, it's the gap between how much code exists in your repo and how much any human on your team genuinely understands. And this is why things like delegation debt end up mattering. You can have a build that passes, you know, your tests, a PR that you can merge, but your team can still end up losing its ability to actually explain the system that they are shipping to production.

Now, a very real pressure is also how much we delegate. So, agents can now stay inside the system long enough for the human to lose the thread. So, a 30-second run, right, can feel like an interaction, but an hour or a day-scale task, so something long horizon, that's a work stream. And when tasks can end up, you know, lasting that long, especially when you begin running many of them in parallel, review can't just be a glance at the end. It has to become a whole control system.

The second thing to avoid is cognitive surrender. Now, this is when you blindly accept AI's responses. Like, delegation is important cuz delegation says, "Do the work, then show me enough evidence that I can judge it." I still make a judgment in that situation. Surrender is really saying, "Hey, your answer is now my answer before I have formed any opinions myself." Now, Wharton did a study that kind of offers us a warning light here. When AI was wrong, 73% of people still thought that they picked the wrong answer and they felt more sure. So, the failure mode is not using AI, but it's borrowed confidence.

The third thing to avoid is orchestration tax. Now, if you've been in the Bay Area, you will see people who for better or worse are still walking around with their laptops open or talking to you about cloud agents. And we're increasingly trying to run more and more and more in parallel or telling each other that we're shipping with hundreds of agents or thousands of agents. More AI agents running does not mean that there is more of you available. Your cognitive bandwidth does not parallelize. So, every loop that you create ends up causing more decisions to route, merge, verify, and integrate. And the fix is not necessarily fewer agents, but it's about designing your attention like a system. Like where you enter, what you require, what you reuse. You just want to be very intentional about it.

Now, accountability can be a scary word for a lot of people. And I wouldn't be surprised if it made you want to go hide in the bushes and just tell your agent to deal with it. But, accountability is not what remains after agents get good. It's what lets the rest of the whole system scale. If agents can do more work, if they can do it faster and parallel, better than what many of us could do, the scarce thing becomes the ability to explain intent, to inspect evidence, to accept risk, and improve the system when the decision was wrong.

Now, here is the career math. The half-life of an edge might be one model release. Speed, recall, verification, even taste all move as the frontier moves. But, the half-life of a signature, your credibility, your expertise is much longer. And by signature, I really mean the name on the work, the person, the team, the institution, whoever stands behind what's actually shipped. So, skills can earn leverage, accountability can turn leverage into trust.

And this is one of the lines that I want to draw pretty clearly. Agents can choose, they can route, they can merge, they can escalate, they can operate inside policy. And in many systems, you know, they can, they should. But execution and responsibility are very different things. The agent can follow your runbook, but it can't inherit the consequences. When something fails, the question is, who understood the policy? Who accepted the risk and who owns the blast radius?

High agency is something that a lot of us talk about these days as being like this thing that we're looking for when we're hiring. High agency is actively taking ownership of your outcomes. So, knowing when to delegate, when to inspect, when to stop, and when to put your name on the result. High agency in this world is not I personally do everything. You know, that version doesn't really scale. It's not just hustle theater, but it's ownership with judgment attached.

This agency ladder tries to make that a little bit more concrete. At the bottom, you've got someone that flags a problem and leaves it for the system. Higher up, they execute, diagnose, propose, recommend, and resolve. And the rare top movement is discernment. You know, maybe you find a problem and you decide whether or not it's worth investing in. Maybe it's not, and maybe you move on. But when agents make more paths possible, agency is not chasing every single path. It's really just deciding which paths deserve your ownership and attention.

So, translate that into an operating model. Agents can run much more of the inner execution loop. They can investigate, implement, test, and report. I think that there's leverage in that, but that outer loop is still engineering. So, deciding, verifying, approving, owning, that inner loop is capability. The outer loop is agency. And this is a boundary that I really care about. Your agent returns evidence. It returns diffs, tests, logs, rationale, traces, trajectories, screenshots, whatever the work itself requires. But then the engineering really begins. We decide whether the work was worth doing. We verify whether the evidence is enough, and we approve or redirect or own what reaches production.

It doesn't matter if you're someone that's just working with a small number of agents, or whether you're working with thousands of agents. I still very much think that these ideas apply. So, the boundary is not human looks at AI output. The boundary is evidence and responsibility. So, here's an operational rule. Explain it or don't ship it. And it's not because humans have to type every line or read every line, but because someone has to understand the work well enough to defend it.

If you've ever worked in a large code base or an enterprise code base, some code bases have this concept of an owners file or certain subdirectories where there are people who are on the hook for that part of the system. You can think about this in a very similar way. Who is accountable for that part of your architecture and your code base? Your model might write the code, and the question is really still whether you can explain those changes that the agent is shipping, whether you've got the evidence where you understand the risks.

Now, this is one of the things I want you to remember near the end. Automation moves the floor for all of us. Engineering continues to move up a level, and our new work might be loop design, evidence design, and brownfield stewardship, but fewer keystrokes doesn't mean less engineering over the next few years. It means that there is more surface area that needs taste, verification, ownership, and ultimately care.

I don't think I've ever been more excited about the future of this field. Every time that we have made it easier to write software, we've predicted that the world would need less of it. And in fact, the opposite happened. Higher-level languages happened, frameworks, cloud, low code. The pattern always went the other way. And when you lower the cost, latent demand ends up appearing. Those ideas that people didn't think were feasible to build and get out there are suddenly unlocked. And agents are going to do the same thing for a lot of people. It's not going to remove engineering work. It's going to move the bottleneck from can we build this to should this exist and can we answer for it? So, build the factories, keep the lights on, own the verdict. I hope this was useful. Thank you.

# How Kepler Built Verifiable AI for Financial Services — Vinoo Ganesh

**Channel:** AI Engineer
**Source:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Tt2kX2sgQio

---

**Vinoo Ganesh:** Hey everyone, thank you for being here. My name is Vinoo Ganesh and I'm the CEO and co-founder of Kepler. Today, I'm going to talk to you about how we built verifiable AI for financial services. First, a little about me. My career has been working in fairly difficult places to work in terms of numerical accuracy and verifiability. I began my career at Palantir where I led the compute platform as well as a lot of our USG engagements. I built and sold an alt data startup, and then was head of business engineering at Citadel. I have some Citadel colleagues here in the audience as well. I've advised a bunch of startups and been lucky that all of them have reached pretty positive outcomes.

This whole talk is a distilled version of a case study Anthropic did on Kepler. If you scan that QR code, we're the only company they've ever done a case study of, which is kind of cool. This has a lot more information about how we were able to do what we do, why it's been pretty impactful in financial services, and really where we go from here. My only goal with this whole talk is to convince you that AI is going to start doing some very powerful things in terms of producing work product. Everything that I tell you is inevitable. Whether it's Kepler or whether it's anyone else, we are already on this journey and this trajectory.

I first want to observe that every talk we've seen in the financial services space so far has been about producing more. Like how do I token max? How do I get AI to do more? Very little of it is about how to actually make AI trustworthy or produce trustworthy products. What's interesting is even terms like trust and verify-ability have actually been largely abused. Evals are not verifiable. You cannot take a non-deterministic LLM and eval your way to something deterministic. These are probability machines.

The underlying reason for this is that AI has made a writing problem a reading problem. We can produce insane amounts of content, whether that's code, whether it's marketing, whether it's like a DCF in record time. But we can't easily verify this. For years the hardest part about this whole process was actually producing the work. Edge and alpha came from people like Citadel being able to hire hundreds of analysts who could scour the internet and understand where any source of alpha could exist. It really came from this idea of being able to consume content. The problem is when a model reads everything, you have the most real version of alpha decay that you possibly can. There is no edge if everyone can look at Tegus and get all the same information.

The hard part now is trusting what actually got produced by the model. This is not necessarily a finance problem; every system that exists has some form of this. In software, we run CICD. We do unit tests, integration tests, and we have code reviews. When a doctor writes a prescription, a pharmacist fills that prescription. So if it says 10,000 milligrams of a medication, someone catches that. We have a pilot and a co-pilot; we have a primary EMT and a secondary. In finance, we have maybe an overworked VP as a verification layer, but that concept doesn't really exist.

I'm going to say something even more aggressive: the reason that people buy products like Bloomberg and FactSet is to displace culpability. When you buy a tool like that, you know that information is free; it exists in SEC filings. But you believe that because a bunch of contractors or folks overseas vetted this data and stuck it in a central instance, at least if it's wrong, everyone on Wall Street has the same incorrect information. That's interesting in certain ways, but it's also kind of a scary proposition. Every one of these tools is read-only. You as an analyst look at Bloomberg, you look at FactSet, you consume information, and you produce the work product. That's where the biggest gap and biggest wall to real meaningful adoption across Wall Street has actually been.

We can't use AI properly in this ecosystem. There is a reason that analysts are still working till 4:00 a.m., and there's a reason folks in investment banks are actually dying because of the hours they're putting in. AI can produce a very confident answer, but when it comes to producing any kind of meaningful work product, we're totally lacking. Not only that, we have the SEC, we have the OCC, and a number of these regulatory agencies who exist to make sure that you are not insider trading, or you're not producing a trading decision that can't be justified or backed by some set of primitives or some set of information that you can reliably say, "I made this decision because of these sources of information."

In this ecosystem, the biggest challenge is how do I get AI to jump from producing the search technologies that it's doing right now to producing work product. That can mean a fairness opinion, it can mean a DCF, it can mean an investment memo, it can mean looking at every SIM that your firm had 5 years ago and figuring out why your IRR number wasn't what it should have been, or anything else. The whole industry has solved this by citing things. When you search the internet with Claude or ChatGPT, it gives you a list of sources that it pulled information from. What's ironic is you can't easily curate those sources. If you find my random Substack that says Palantir is going to be $3,000 a share and you trade off of that, please go do that because it'll be very helpful for me. But that's not a real vetted source. Seeking Alpha and some of these blogs or Reddit posts are data points, but they're not real vetted sources.

Showing where you got the information from is only half the battle. The citation is effectively an after-the-fact audit. Now, a verification is a deterministic, repeatable, numerically verifiable mechanism that we can use to produce validity that a number is right. A verification just means I can prove deterministically this number is right. So, when I extract a revenue number from a 10-K, I can deterministically prove that is the correct number from that 10-K. These are two sides of the same game: one is showing where you got the sources from, and one is verifying that the information that you pulled out is actually correct.

This becomes challenging because verification is not an outcome. It lives in the path or the set of steps that are required for you to produce information that is valid for your individual firm. Finance is one of the rare industries where two people can have the same information, and one can be long a stock, and one can be short that stock with the exact same data. The idea of verification is not actually ground truth. It is verifying that you got an output that respects the nouns and verbs or the rules of your organization. If a TMT desk at Citadel believes that a particular stock is going to go up into the right, another TMT desk at Citadel may have the exact opposite belief, and they may have the same verification mechanisms that produce vastly different outcomes.

This comes down to something simple: What are the sources that we trust? What are the transformations that we apply on those sources to produce information that we care about? And how do we make sure that's codified in a way that makes logical sense? The point is that "this came from a 10-K" is not the validation as a whole. Your job now is to figure out as an individual: how do I use AI in a verifiable way? Here's the honest answer: You don't. AI is great at doing non-deterministic tasks. It can solve problems in a way that's novel. It can figure out exactly how to do EBITDA adjustments, but it can't be the one responsible for doing the mathematical adjustments because it's a probability machine. It is great at next token prediction.

The second contention of this whole talk is that you cannot use AI to produce verifiable work product in finance without augmenting it with a deterministic substrate. This effectively means, if you're a portfolio manager at Citadel, you have access to a number of deterministic tools that you use to make your trading decisions. We need to model AI like that PM. It needs to exist in grounding, needs to exist with a certain risk threshold and verifiability.

Here's how we did it. We have three tenants that we use to ensure that numerical accuracy is a tenant of the Kepler platform. The first is atomic provenance, the second is scope determinism, and the third is derivation chains. The core premise is this: there are certain things humans should never do. I don't believe a human should sit there and look at a PDF 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, or earnings call transcript and on one screen take that number and put it into an Excel model on the other screen. Humans were not built for that.

Let's talk about provenance. Provenance as a whole just means writing down exactly where you got the information. We trained a model that was really good at extracting information. It outperformed foundation models, it's 94% great—it's in the article. Who here would trade off of something that's 94% accurate? Fine-tuning your way on probabilistic solutions is really cool and TechCrunch will be really excited about it, but no one else really cares about it, because a wrong number is still wrong if you're in that unfortunate 6%.

With atomic provenance, what we do is the model writes effectively a reference to the number. It cannot write the number or manipulate the number in any way. It doesn't even understand what that number is. We have tools that are really good at understanding numbers—they're databases, systems that can codify information and read them and write them with appropriate fidelity. Anytime a model makes a decision, it makes the decision to figure out exactly where it got the number from and hand off to something that can write that number. We then run it through a deterministic check where any kind of a wrong number, if we can't verify it independently, we strip it out. That number will never make it to someone if it doesn't follow the deterministic check, the provenance ledger, and most importantly, the whole cycle repeating at least a couple of times. This is not me saying have 10 models and have OpenAI check ChatGPT and have Anthropic check xAI. These are not probabilistic systems evaluating each other's work. There's a core canonical process of extracting a number, persisting it, and making sure that process actually occurred properly. This is what I mean by atomic, like traditional atomicity in database land.

Second is scope determinism. This was a super controversial idea like a year ago, and VCs were like, "This is crazy." Now, the model is really good at reasoning and planning. Intelligence is commoditized. GLM 52 shows it; you can download it off of Hugging Face right now. You have something as powerful as Opus 48. What the model cannot do is math. And why would it? Why would I run 1 + 1 through a multi-billion parameter model instead of one CPU cycle? Unless you're companies that are giving bonuses on people token maxing, which is another Polarys thing.

The model decides what to compute; it never does the computation itself. From the Kepler platform perspective, we split the deterministic pieces of the model, which are none, from the non-deterministic pieces of the model, which are all of them. We give the model the right tooling and technology to calculate the deterministic pieces. To get concrete, a model can read something like, "Okay, I need to understand what net margin is." I know the right pieces of information to go to to get that data, but I can't be the entity that's actually running the code behind the scenes to pull that number out of a PDF or parsing the XBRL behind the scenes. That is code. The deterministic pieces of the platform pull that information out and persist it outside of anything the model understands. Together, we can produce a numerically accurate answer to the question of what was the net margin of this stock or this company last quarter. This is also a lot cheaper because I don't need the model to do a bunch of stuff it shouldn't be doing.

The last piece here is how do we actually do reconciliation? When someone asks about a ratio like a gross margin or anything else that doesn't exist in a filing, I can't just go look up what the gross margin is or what the set of EBITDA adjustments were. Everyone calculates these ratios and these multiples differently. Everyone does enterprise value calculations differently. Things that are considered recurring or non-recurring may be unique. We not only have to codify that in the processes that are run, but we need some kind of a chain of events to figure out what went into producing an individual number and what went into producing an outcome. This is not any different than the chain of events that an analyst does on a desk at a hedge fund to make a risk-reward or a trading decision. It's just done by the model in a way that can be replayed and rewound.

We have a system that knows which data points it's allowed to produce—meaning from structured filings, from numerical data, from any other ecosystem—and it knows what it's never allowed to produce. If it's pulling things out of prose, raw tables, or anything else, it doesn't do that extraction. This allows us to do things like consolidate financial statements in seconds with every number tied back to its individual source. This means that companies like the CapIQs and the Deloopas that are all using contractors for this, we don't need to do that anymore. We can actually create a financial model in a numerically accurate way that allows you to build work product. We can build a DCF in the format that you actually want; the model will not hallucinate that a row exists that shouldn't exist.

Everything that I'm telling you generally generalizes past finance. We're picking numbers here because finance cares about numbers, but you can imagine a world where every court case, if you're a Harvey or a Legora, runs through the same process: a pre-processing step that understands that we can extract entities like case A versus case B and store that deterministically so we don't hallucinate citations. Or every drug discovery formulation that exists in NIH white papers such that we never miss a compound.

We are in an ecosystem right now where we're almost like pre-SSL in the e-commerce ecosystem. What's the TAM of e-commerce? Trillions. But how many people were comfortable putting their credit card number on the internet before there was security? Zero. We're in the last step. AI can now produce verifiable work product across a number of industries. The rag platforms of the past are really helpful and cool in codifying workflows, but there's a reason that the foundational labs are going after every one of these. There's a reason that Claude for science is not a deterministic system, but still a rag-based system. The piece that should be really exciting is that there is a piece of this that no one has built yet in a variety of disciplines and industries.

We're really good at consuming tokens. In fact, there's a club here for people that consumed a billion plus tokens; they're walking around with gold cards. In what time in history has an employee been rewarded for your company to pay another vendor for how much money you're spending? Token maxing is now being thought of as not the right approach to solve your problems. The natural thing will become a rush to the bottom, which is an optimization problem. If you rewind time, I sat on this stage 4 years ago talking about Snowflake Summit and Databricks Summit, where the idea was all of a sudden people wanted ROI on top of their Snowflake investment or their Databricks investment. We started doing cost optimization to make sure every dollar of capital we put into Snowflake and into Databricks went to actually producing a pipeline that people were using. That same trend is about to start. We're figuring out right now how do we use the right tool for the right job. Sometimes you don't need a multi-billion parameter model when one CPU cycle will just work.

To wrap this up, AI has made producing work nearly free—thank you VCs, heavily subsidized. The reading problem is still very open. Verifying a data point is not enough anymore; the system has to be able to track its own provenance and ensure that the numbers that you're pulling represent your own unique company philosophies. Citations got us 50% of the way there, but the next half of the verifiability and provability is going to be how we start using this in real, valuable, verifiable work. The work product itself is the proof. In code, we have unit tests, pull requests, and every commit and code review stored in perpetuity. There are companies here trying to mine that information to create a representation of your ontology on a company-specific basis. We need that same ecosystem in finance.

All these problems are solved at this point. The last remaining mile is going to be that personalization. The second version of this in 2027 will hopefully see one of us on stage talking about how we're now able to build verifiable ontologies that actually proxy our investment processes instead of saying how do I not spend a trillion tokens to solve this individual problem. Susanna and I are both from Kepler. We're growing pretty quickly; come join us if these problems are interesting to you. We're starting in finance now, but we'll be in a lot of different dimensions pretty quickly. Thank you so much and happy to answer any questions.

**Guest:** Yes, your question is about provenance and from the provenance ledger, where does the number actually come from?

**Vinoo Ganesh:** At its core, the number comes from three different things. It comes from extracted information from the filings. It comes from either a mathematical calculation that we do to derivative production, so like a ratio or something else. Or it comes from your internal documents or other internal pieces of information that operate in conjunction with that external data to produce that individual data point. Anytime the model effectively is responsible for telling some entity to do an IO operation, that's part of the provenance chain.

**Guest:** What are your customers most excited about in your product?

**Vinoo Ganesh:** It's funny. Everyone wants AI—the dream is the AI portfolio manager. The portfolio managers don't want the AI portfolio manager; they want the AI analyst. The thing they're most excited about is a way of rapidly doing the repeatable painful tasks that their analysts are doing. Things like when an analyst sits there and listens to an earnings call transcript; if we didn't have to have an analyst do that, it would be amazing. Or an analyst sits there with 15 tabs and they're opening every 8-K and 10-K over the last few years to create the V0 of a financial model. They're most excited about getting their analyst time back. That's the honest answer. And these are expensive analysts—some of these folks make 600-700k a year to do this. I'm happy to answer any more questions outside as well.
